name: Honeygar

card.summary: Honeygar is a honey-and-vinegar tonic drunk as a daily wellness drink, tied by fans to digestion, weight and skin they hope will look better.
card.aka: Honey and vinegar drink, honegar, oxymel
card.note: Vinegar is acidic; sipping it undiluted is commonly associated with tooth-enamel and throat irritation.

quick.overview:
Honeygar is a mix of honey and vinegar, usually diluted in water and drunk as a tonic. It is a modern, informal relative of oxymel, an old honey-and-vinegar preparation.

People take it for general wellness, digestion and weight, with a clearer-skin or leaner-look payoff implied. Small clinical trials on oxymel have looked at chronic conditions including obesity, with sample sizes too small to settle the question [1].
quick.how: Honey and vinegar are stirred into water and sipped, often mornings or before meals. It is combined with other wellness habits.
quick.risks: Vinegar is acidic and may irritate teeth and throat if taken strong; honey adds sugar and should not be given to infants. People on diabetes or heart medicines are typically advised by clinicians to ask before regular use.

lead: Honeygar is an informal name for a drink made from honey and vinegar. Its ancestor is oxymel, a blend of honey and vinegar described by Cato the Elder and carried through Renaissance pharmacopoeias [1].

Users drink it as a general tonic, hoping for steadier digestion, appetite control and clearer skin, so that weight and complexion look better. These links are claimed by practitioners rather than established.

angle.text: Fans sip it as part of a daily routine, expecting gradual benefits for weight and skin. Appearance effects are indirect and reported anecdotally.

paras: Oxymel, from the Latin for acid and honey, was described by Cato the Elder, later repeated by Columella, and listed in Renaissance and later pharmacopoeias; a 1593 surgical text recommended it in an eye-inflammation treatment [1]. The term honegar or honeygar does not appear in that history; it is a modern informal label.

Clinical trials of oxymel have examined chronic conditions including obesity; the encyclopedic summary notes small sample sizes and a need for more research [1]. No studies found specifically on honeygar for appearance.
